This study presents an analysis of EPEs across the full annual cycle of the Himalayas from 1979 to 2023, identifying their spatial and seasonal distributions and associated precursor weather regimes. Based on the frequency of seasonal EPEs, the Himalayas are categorized into winter\u2010dominated (Karakoram, WH, and northwest Central Himalayas [CH]) and summer\u2010dominated (CH to Eastern Himalayas [EH]). By clustering circulation fields during EPEs, six dominant weather regimes are identified: four monsoon\u2010driven (Bay of Bengal Low\u2010Pressure System [BoB\u2010LPS], Arabian Sea LPS [AS\u2010LPS], Monsoon\u2010Break, and Western\u2010Disturbance Monsoon [WD\u2010Monsoon]) and two winter\u2010driven (WH\u2010WD and CH\u2010WD). Each regime exhibits a distinct atmospheric circulation pattern. The BoB\u2010LPS and AS\u2010LPS regimes are characterized by quasi\u2010stationary blocking by an anomalous upper\u2010level anticyclone situated over the WH along with the LPS formed over the BoB and AS, respectively. The Monsoon\u2010Break cluster reflects a weakened monsoon trough and suppressed convection over the BoB and core monsoon regions. In contrast, the WH\u2010WD and CH\u2010WD clusters are associated with upper\u2010level cyclonic anomalies characteristic of WDs, embedded within broader wave\u2010train\u2010like circulation anomalies that are consistent with previously reported North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO)\u2013subtropical jet (STJ)\u2013WD pathways. There is a spatial dipole in composite precipitation: EPEs in monsoon\u2010driven clusters are associated with anomalous moisture transport from the BoB and AS, which results in dry conditions in the winter\u2010dominated Himalayas, while EPEs in WD\u2010driven regimes result from anomalous westerly moisture flow from the AS and associated dry conditions in the summer\u2010dominated Himalayas. This study offers a synoptic\u2010scale framework for interpreting the circulation regimes associated with Himalayan EPEs and for identifying conditions that may be favourable for their occurrence.<\/jats:p>","DOI":"10.1002\/qj.70308","type":"journal-article","created":{"date-parts":[[2026,9,17]],"date-time":"2026-09-17T09:02:17Z","timestamp":1789635737000},"update-policy":"https:\/\/doi.org\/10.1002\/crossmark_policy","source":"Crossref","is-referenced-by-count":0,"title":["Synoptic and large\u2010scale drivers of extreme precipitation events in the Himalayas"],"prefix":"10.1002","author":[{"ORCID":"https:\/\/orcid.org\/0009-0003-8223-9399","authenticated-orcid":false,"given":"Priya","family":"Bharati","sequence":"first","affiliation":[{"name":"Centre for Ocean, River, Atmosphere and Land Sciences (CORAL) Indian Institute of Technology Kharagpur  Kharagpur India"},{"name":"Department of Atmospheric Sciences National Taiwan University  Taipei Taiwan"}],"role":[{"vocabulary":"crossref","role":"author"}]},{"ORCID":"https:\/\/orcid.org\/0000-0002-1858-0918","authenticated-orcid":false,"given":"Pranab","family":"Deb","sequence":"additional","affiliation":[{"name":"Centre for Ocean, River, Atmosphere and Land Sciences (CORAL) Indian Institute of Technology Kharagpur  Kharagpur India"}],"role":[{"vocabulary":"crossref","role":"author"}]},{"ORCID":"https:\/\/orcid.org\/0000-0003-1480-3755","authenticated-orcid":false,"given":"Kieran M.
